text: Halfway through a hard maths problem, an AI stopped, and wrote this.
Wait, wait. Wait. That’s an aha moment I can flag here.
Hold on. It said that by itself? Nobody told it to say wait?
Nobody. It had only ever been given problems, a simple template, and a score.
So the AI taught itself to reason? That’s amazing!
Partly. But a later paper found the story was more ordinary. Part of it was a quirk in the maths.
A quirk? Okay, now I need to know.
By the end, you’ll know what really grew, and the setting that controls it.
The aha moment. Episode one.
So what did they give it? Examples of good reasoning?
None at all. Picture an exam paper with two boxes printed on it.
A big box for your working, and a small box for the final answer.
The examiner only marks the small box. But they check you used both.
So it’s told where to think, but not how to think.
In the real thing, the boxes are tags. The working goes inside think tags, and the answer inside answer tags.
Then two rules grade it. Accuracy: is the final answer right?
And format: did it use the tags? Both are checked by plain code.
Why not get another AI to grade the answers? Like a judge?
DeepSeek avoided that. Watch. Tiny gives a wrong answer, very confidently. And the judge loves it.
Oh no. So it learns to fool the judge, not to do maths.
That’s reward hacking. A few lines of code that check the answer are much harder to fool.
And it worked. On a hard competition maths test called AIME...
R1-Zero started out solving fifteen point six percent of the problems, on one try.
And by the end?
Seventy-one percent. And with a majority vote over many tries, eighty-six point seven.
Something else happened at the same time. The answers got longer.
Early on: a few lines, often a guess.
Later: longer working, then checking, then trying another way.
But nobody rewarded length, right? Only the answer and the tags.
Right. Longer working got more answers right, so it got reinforced. From hundreds of tokens, to thousands.
Then, partway through a hard algebra problem, came the famous moment.
Wait, wait. Wait. That’s an aha moment I can flag here.
Then it went back and re-checked its own working.
So that’s reasoning appearing out of nowhere. Right?
That’s how the story was told. Then a 2025 paper took a closer look.
People call it the Dr. GRPO paper.
First finding: base models, before any reinforcement learning, already show this aha-style self-checking.
Wait. So the training didn’t invent it?
Not invented. Found. The model already did it sometimes, and training made it much more common.
Like a radio station that was always on, just very quiet. Training turned up the volume.
Second finding. And it’s about how the blame gets shared out.
Two wrong answers get the same penalty. One is ten words long, one is a hundred. Each penalty is spread over that answer’s own words.
So which one gets off lighter, per word?
Pause, and have a guess.
C! Wrong is wrong. Same penalty, so length shouldn’t matter. Right?
It feels fair. But no. It’s B. The long wrong answer gets off lighter.
Think of butter. One knob of butter on one slice of toast makes a thick layer.
Spread the same knob over ten slices, and each one barely tastes of it.
The penalty is the butter. The words are the slices. Ten words: each word gets a tenth.
A hundred words: each word gets a hundredth. Ten times gentler.
Oh no. So when it’s not sure, rambling is the safer bet!
Exactly. Over thousands of steps, wrong answers drift longer.
So some of that famous growth was just butter, spreading.
The fix is called Dr. GRPO. GRPO done right.
Divide every answer by the same fixed number, not by its own length. Now a word counts the same, in a short reply or a long one.
And scale rewards, none? What’s that one?
A second, smaller bias the paper found. Switch that off too.
Some growth is real. Hard problems need more working. So, always watch length and accuracy together.
Picture a run where the answers keep getting longer.
But accuracy just sits there, flat.
That’s not an aha moment. That’s butter.
Right. Then read the replies. A real check looks very different from filler.
Quick recap.
R1-Zero got two boxes, and two rules: is it right, and did it use the tags.
The aha habit was already there. Training made it common.
And some of the length growth was just the penalty, spread thin.
But even with the bias fixed, all this thinking has a cost.
Ask a freshly trained reasoning model what two plus three is, and you might get this.
Three paragraphs? Two hundred tokens, to say five?!
And every one of those tokens costs time and money.
So how do we make it think less, without making it dumber?
That’s the next episode.
